html:
The habit of drinking coffee, which began among Sufi Muslims in Yemen by the middle of the 1400s. They brewed roasted coffee beans into a drink called qahwa and drank it to stay awake through long night prayers.

The coffee shrub grows wild in the highlands of Ethiopia, across the Red Sea. Yemenis began to grow it on terraced mountain slopes, and for about two centuries Yemen supplied nearly all the world's coffee. Early writers credit local Sufi teachers in Aden and the port of Mocha with making it popular. The full story of how coffee arrived is told under Coffee reaches Yemen.

From Sufi lodges the drink spread to Mecca, to students at Al-Azhar in Cairo, and by the 1550s to the coffeehouses of Istanbul. Scholars argued over whether it was an intoxicant forbidden by Islam, and Mecca banned it briefly in 1511. Exports through the Mocha trade made Yemen rich until the Dutch began growing coffee in Java around 1700.
